items.prompt: What is the mean of a data set?

options.label: The middle value once the data are sorted in order
The sum of all values divided by the number of values
The value that occurs most often in the data set
The largest value in the data minus the smallest value

rubric: The mean is the sum divided by the count.
Distractors describe the median, mode and range.

items.prompt: What is the median of 2, 4, 6, 8, 100?
rubric: The middle value of the five ordered numbers is 6.
24 is the mean, which the outlier pulls upward.

items.prompt: Which of these is a measure of spread?

options.label: Median
Standard deviation
Mode
Mean

rubric: Standard deviation measures how spread out values are.
The others measure center.

items.prompt: Which chart is typically used to show the distribution of one numerical variable, such as exam scores?

options.label: Histogram
Line chart
Scatterplot
Pie chart

rubric: A histogram groups numeric values into bins to show distribution.
A scatterplot needs two variables; pie charts show category shares.

items.prompt: In statistics, what is a sample?

options.label: A single value chosen as the typical one in the data
The complete group of everyone we want to study
A summary number that describes a whole population
A subset of the population that is actually observed

rubric: A sample is the part of the population that is observed.
The first option describes the population; the third describes a parameter.

items.prompt: Which of the following are measures of center? Select all that apply.

options.label: Standard deviation
Mode
Mean
Median
Range

rubric: Mean, median and mode are measures of center.
Range and standard deviation measure spread.

items.prompt: A school has 800 students numbered 1 to 800. A researcher uses a random number generator to pick 80 different numbers and surveys the students with those numbers. What is this sampling method called?

options.label: Simple random sample
Voluntary response sample
Stratified sample
Convenience sample

rubric: Every student has an equal chance of selection, which defines a simple random sample.
Stratified sampling requires splitting into groups first.

items.prompt: House prices in a town are right-skewed because of a few very expensive homes. How do the mean and median compare?

options.label: The two cannot be compared, because the data are skewed
The mean equals the median, because skew affects neither of them
The mean is larger than the median, pulled up by the high values
The mean is smaller than the median, pulled down by cheap homes

rubric: High values pull the mean above the median in right-skewed data.
Distractors reverse the direction or deny the effect of skew.

items.prompt: A 95% confidence interval for a population mean is 40 to 46. Which interpretation is correct?

options.label: The true mean varies from sample to sample and stays between 40 and 46 about 95% of the time
There is a 95% chance that any single new observation will fall between 40 and 46
Intervals built this way capture the true mean in about 95% of repeated samples
About 95% of the individual values in the population lie between 40 and 46

rubric: The 95% describes the long-run success rate of the method.
Distractors treat the interval as covering individual values or treat the mean as random.

items.prompt: What happens to the standard error of the mean when the sample size increases, other things equal?

options.label: It stays the same, because it depends only on the population
It becomes zero once the sample exceeds 30 values
It increases, because more data adds more variation
It decreases, because averages of more values vary less

rubric: Standard error shrinks roughly with the square root of n.
Distractors confuse sample size with variability or invent a cutoff.

items.prompt: Why is the median often preferred to the mean when summarizing incomes that include a few extremely high earners?

options.label: The median is resistant to extreme values, so it reflects a typical income
The median is usually larger than the mean, so it gives a fairer picture of income
The median is easier to compute for large data sets, so it is used with income data
The median uses every value in the data, so it is more precise for skewed data

rubric: The median is not pulled by extreme values.
The first distractor is false: the mean uses every value; the median uses position.

items.prompt: Across months, ice cream sales and drownings have a correlation of 0.8. What is the best interpretation?

options.label: The relationship is weak, because 0.8 is below 1
Ice cream sales cause drownings, because the correlation is strong
Drownings cause ice cream sales to rise, because r is positive
They tend to rise together, but this alone does not show causation

rubric: Correlation shows association; a lurking variable such as hot weather may explain both.
Distractors infer causation or misread the size of r.

items.prompt: Which statements about standard deviation are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: It is zero when all values are identical
It can be negative when most values are below the mean
It is measured in the same units as the data
A larger value means the data are more spread out
It always equals the mean divided by the sample size

rubric: Standard deviation measures spread in the data's units and is zero only with no variation.
It is never negative and is not mean divided by n.

items.prompt: A poll of 1,000 voters finds 52% support a measure, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3 points at 95% confidence. What is the best interpretation?

options.label: Exactly 52% of all voters support it, but about 3% of the individual answers given were recorded wrongly
Support in the population plausibly lies from 49% to 55%, so a majority is uncertain
The measure will pass, because 52% is above the 50% line and the poll sampled 1,000 voters
Three percent of the 1,000 voters sampled declined to answer, so the result covers only 97% of them

rubric: The margin of error gives a plausible range that includes values below 50%.
Distractors treat the sample figure as exact or misread the margin of error.

items.prompt: Why is the median often preferred to the mean when summarising household incomes in a region?

options.label: It is simpler to compute, since it needs no sorting or adding
It uses every value in the data, so it is more precise overall
It always lands close to the mean once samples are large enough
A few extremely high incomes barely move it, unlike the mean

rubric: The median depends on the middle position, so extreme incomes in a right-skewed distribution hardly affect it.
Distractors confuse robustness with using every value, or assume mean and median agree in large samples.

items.prompt: Two classes both have a mean test score of 70. Class A has a standard deviation of 5 and class B has a standard deviation of 15. What does this tell you?

options.label: Class B scores have a higher typical value than class A
Class B scores are more spread out around the mean
Class A scores are more spread out around the mean
Class A has more students than class B does

rubric: Standard deviation measures spread around the mean, so the larger value means more variability.
Distractors mix up spread with centre or with sample size.

items.prompt: Why does a voluntary online poll, where anyone may choose to respond, often give biased results?

options.label: Online polls always end up with too few responses to be useful
People who choose to respond tend to differ from those who do not
Random selection cannot be used for any question asked online
Voluntary responses make the margin of error exactly zero

rubric: Self-selection makes the respondents unrepresentative of the population, which causes bias.
Distractors blame sample size or the online medium rather than the selection mechanism.

items.prompt: A 95% confidence interval for a population mean is 48 to 56. Which is the best interpretation?

options.label: There is a 95% chance the sample mean itself lies from 48 to 56
Intervals built this way capture the true mean in about 95% of samples
About 95% of the individual values in the population lie from 48 to 56
95% of all future sample means will fall between 48 and 56

rubric: Confidence refers to the long-run capture rate of the method for the true parameter.
Distractors treat the interval as a range for individual values, for the sample mean, or for future sample means.

items.prompt: The sample size is quadrupled while the population standard deviation stays the same. What happens to the standard error of the sample mean?

options.label: It stays the same
It is doubled
It is halved
It is quartered

rubric: Standard error is sigma divided by the square root of n, so quadrupling n halves it.
Quartering comes from forgetting the square root.

items.prompt: Which statements about a histogram are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: Bar heights show counts or frequencies of values within each bin
Gaps between bars always mean that data are missing
It is the usual chart for unordered categories such as favourite colour
It shows the shape of the distribution of a numerical variable

rubric: Histograms bin numerical data and show frequency by bar height, revealing shape.
Unordered categories call for a bar chart, and gaps simply mean empty bins.

items.prompt: A fitness app company surveys users who logged at least one workout last month. It finds that 80% exercise weekly, and plans to advertise that 80% of all adults exercise weekly. What is the main problem with this claim?

options.label: Weekly exercise is categorical, so no percentage can describe it
The survey should have asked about the last year instead of one month
The sample is large, which makes percentages unreliable for adults
The sample holds only active users, so it likely overstates adult exercise

rubric: The sample is drawn from a non-representative subgroup, causing selection bias when generalising to all adults.
Distractors invent problems with sample size, with percentages for categories, or with the time window.

items.prompt: What is the mean of the data set 4, 8, 6, 10, 12?
rubric: Sum is 40, divided by 5 gives 8.
Other values come from the median of a miscounted list or arithmetic slips.

items.prompt: What is the median of the data set 3, 9, 4, 12, 7, 5?
rubric: Sorted: 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 12. With an even count, average 5 and 7 to get 6.
Learners who skip sorting or pick one middle value get 5 or 7.

items.prompt: Exam scores have mean 70 and standard deviation 5. What is the z-score of a score of 85?
rubric: 15 forgets to divide by the SD; 0.33 inverts the ratio.

items.prompt: A sample of n = 100 has a sample standard deviation of 20. What is the estimated standard error of the mean?
rubric: 10 divides by n over 10 mistakenly; 20 ignores sample size; 0.2 divides by n.

items.prompt: A sample mean is 50 with a standard error of 2. Using about 2 standard errors, what is an approximate 95% confidence interval?
rubric: 48 to 52 uses one SE; 44 to 56 uses three; 50 to 54 is one-sided.

items.prompt: For the data set 2, 3, 3, 4, 18, which statistics equal 3? Select all that apply.

options.label: The range
The median
The mean
The mode

rubric: The middle value and most frequent value are both 3.
The mean is 6, pulled up by 18, and the range is 16.

items.prompt: A random survey of 400 voters finds that 220 favour a proposal, so the sample proportion is 0.55. The standard error is about sqrt(0.55 × 0.45 / 400), which is roughly 0.025. Using about 2 standard errors, which interval is an approximate 95% confidence interval for the population proportion?
rubric: 0.525 to 0.575 uses one SE; 0.45 to 0.65 uses four; the last is one-sided.

items.prompt: A sample of n = 36 has mean 50 and standard deviation 12. Using z = 1.96, what is the approximate 95% confidence interval for the population mean?
rubric: 26.48 to 73.52 uses the standard deviation instead of the standard error; 48.04 to 51.96 divides by 12 instead of 6.

items.prompt: Exam scores are roughly normal with mean 70 and standard deviation 8. Using the 68-95-99.7 rule, about what percentage of students score above 86?

options.label: About 2.5%
About 16%
About 0.15%
About 5%

rubric: 86 is 2 SDs above the mean; 95% lie within 2 SDs, leaving 2.5% in the upper tail.
5% forgets that the tail is split in two; 16% is the 1 SD tail.

items.prompt: A pollster has no prior estimate of a proportion and wants a 95% margin of error of at most 0.03. Using z = 1.96 and the conservative p = 0.5, what is the minimum sample size?
rubric: 385 corresponds to a 0.05 margin; 534 halves the answer; 2135 doubles it.

items.prompt: A data set has Q1 = 20 and Q3 = 32. Using the 1.5 x IQR rule, what is the upper fence beyond which values are flagged as outliers?
rubric: The other values come from adding 0.5, 1 or 2 times the IQR instead of 1.5.

items.prompt: In a 2x2 table of 200 people, one row total is 60 and one column total is 40. Under independence, what is the expected count in the cell where that row and column meet?
rubric: Expected = row total x column total / grand total = 60 x 40 / 200 = 12.
The distractors come from dividing by the wrong totals or splitting counts evenly.

items.prompt: A population has standard deviation 10, and samples of n = 25 are drawn. Which statements about the sampling distribution of the sample mean are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: Its standard error is 2.
Raising n to 100 would cut the standard error to 1.
Raising n to 100 would cut the standard error to 0.5.
Its standard error is 0.4.
Its standard error is 10 whatever n is.

rubric: SE = 10/sqrt(25) = 2, and with n = 100 it is 10/10 = 1.
Distractors divide by n instead of sqrt(n), or treat the SE as unchanged by sample size.

items.prompt: A council surveys a simple random sample of 400 residents about a new bus route. 120 residents say they support it. The analyst wants a 95% confidence interval for the population proportion, using z = 1.96 and the normal approximation.
rubric: 20.1% to 39.9% omits the division by n; the narrower intervals shrink the SE wrongly.

items.prompt: Treatment A has a higher recovery rate than B in both mild and severe patient groups, yet B has the higher overall recovery rate. What is the most likely explanation?

options.label: A was given mostly to severe patients, so group mix distorts the pooled rate
B's subgroup samples were larger, so its subgroup rates are more precise and its pooled rate is more trustworthy
The pooled rate is an unweighted average of subgroup rates, so it should favour A if A wins in each subgroup
Recovery rates from mild and severe groups are on different scales, so they should not be combined

rubric: Simpson's paradox: unequal group sizes (confounding by severity) can reverse the pooled comparison.
The 'average' distractor ignores that pooled rates are weighted by group size, which differs between treatments.

items.prompt: A right-skewed data set has mean 52 and median 41. What does this gap most plausibly indicate?

options.label: The standard deviation must be smaller than the 11-point gap, since the mean and median differ by so little
A few very large values pull the mean up while the median stays near the typical value
The median is miscalculated, because in skewed data the median should equal the mean
Roughly half the values are above 52, because the mean marks the midpoint of the ordered data

rubric: Large values in the right tail raise the mean but barely affect the median.
The midpoint distractor confuses the mean with the median.

items.prompt: An analyst compares 20 customer segments to a control at alpha = 0.05, finds one with p = 0.03, and reports a real effect for that segment. What is the main flaw?

options.label: Running 20 tests makes about one false positive likely by chance, so one p = 0.03 is weak evidence
Each segment needs more than 30 observations before any single test result can be counted as valid
A p-value of 0.03 is above the cutoff once the test is made two-sided, so it cannot be called significant
Segments are compared with one control, so a paired test was needed instead of an unpaired comparison

rubric: Multiple comparisons inflate the chance of at least one false positive; an adjustment is needed.
Reading p = 0.03 in isolation ignores how many tests were run.

items.prompt: A researcher adds 50 more observations to a sample of 30 and recomputes a 95% CI for the mean. The interval gets wider. Which explanation is most plausible?

options.label: The new observations were much more variable, so the larger SD outweighed the larger n
The confidence level rose automatically as the sample grew, and a higher level gives a wider interval
The sample mean moved noticeably after adding the data, and any shift in the mean widens the interval
Extra observations add noise, so a larger sample gives a wider interval whatever their spread

rubric: Width depends on s/sqrt(n); a big rise in s can outweigh the gain from n.
Distractors confuse the mean's location with the interval's width or claim n widens intervals.

items.prompt: A scatterplot shows a clear U-shaped relationship between two variables, yet the correlation coefficient is r = 0.04. Which diagnosis is best?

options.label: The sample is too small, since a real relationship of this clear shape would still give a large r
A U-shape means the slope is negative on average, so r should be strongly negative
An r near 0 shows the variables are independent, so the pattern must be chance
The relationship is real, but r only measures linear association, so a curve can give r near 0

rubric: Pearson r captures only linear association; symmetric curves cancel out.
Equating r near 0 with independence is the common misconception.

items.prompt: Which features of a survey design are likely to introduce bias into an estimate of public opinion (not just imprecision)? Select all that apply.

options.label: The phone directory used excludes households with only mobile phones
A simple random sample of only 100 people is drawn
Nonresponse is much higher among people who hold one particular view
Respondents choose themselves by clicking a link on a website
A proportional stratified random sample is used

rubric: Self-selection, a flawed sampling frame and opinion-related nonresponse all shift estimates systematically.
A small random sample is imprecise but unbiased; proportional stratification does not add bias.

items.prompt: In an A/B test, version A converts 20 of 500 visitors (4.0%) and version B converts 22 of 500 (4.4%). A manager says B is clearly better. The standard error of the difference is about 1.3 percentage points.

options.label: B is clearly better, because its conversion rate is higher in the sample and the groups are the same size
The test is invalid, because equal group sizes of 500 hide differences between the two versions
The 0.4-point gap is only about 0.3 SE, so it is well within sampling variation
The gap is significant, because both conversion rates are low and so B's lead is unlikely to be chance

rubric: 0.4 / 1.3 is about 0.3 SE, so the data are consistent with no true difference.
A higher sample rate alone does not establish a real difference; equal group sizes are not a flaw.

items.prompt: Drug A has a higher recovery rate than Drug B within Hospital 1 and within Hospital 2, yet B has the higher recovery rate when the hospitals are pooled. What best explains this?

options.label: The pooled rate is an error because rates cannot be combined across hospitals
Drug A must work worse overall because pooled data always outrank subgroup data
Drug B was mostly given in the hospital with milder cases, so group mix drives the pooled rate
The within-hospital results are probably due to chance because they use smaller samples

rubric: This is Simpson's paradox: unequal allocation of a confounder (case mix or hospital) reverses the pooled comparison.
Distractors wrongly assume pooled data always beat subgroups or dismiss subgroup results as chance.

items.prompt: A company reports mean salary 52k and median salary 38k for 400 employees. What does the gap most plausibly indicate about the distribution?

options.label: A symmetric distribution, since the mean and median both measure the centre
Right skew, as a few very high salaries pull the mean above the median
Left skew, as the many salaries below the median pull the mean upward and away from it
Outliers on the low end, which drag the median down while leaving the mean unaffected

rubric: The mean is sensitive to extreme high values, so mean greater than median suggests right skew.
Distractors confuse the direction of skew or assume mean and median must agree.

items.prompt: A pilot study with n = 50 gives a 95% CI for a mean with margin of error 6. Assuming a similar standard deviation, roughly what sample size gives a margin of error of 3?

options.label: About 100, because halving the margin needs double the data
About 200, because the margin shrinks with the square root of n
About 150, because each extra 50 observations cuts 2 points of margin
About 400, because the margin shrinks with the fourth root of n

rubric: Margin of error is proportional to 1/sqrt(n), so halving it needs four times the sample.
Distractors assume a linear or wrongly-powered relationship between n and precision.

items.prompt: A researcher tests the link between a supplement and 20 different health outcomes, each at the 0.05 level, and reports one significant result (p = 0.04) as a finding. What is the main flaw in this analysis?

options.label: A p-value of 0.04 is too close to the 0.05 cutoff, so it cannot be counted as significant
Running 20 outcomes makes the sample too large, and that makes every p-value unreliable here
With 20 tests, about one false positive is expected by chance, so one hit is weak evidence
Testing many outcomes lowers the power of each test, so the one significant result is invalid

rubric: Multiple comparisons inflate the familywise error rate; roughly 1 in 20 true-null tests is significant by chance.
Distractors misread the threshold or confuse multiplicity with sample size or power.

items.prompt: An online poll with 20,000 self-selected respondents shows 70% support for a policy. A random sample of 1,000 voters shows 52%. Why is the larger poll likely the less accurate one?

options.label: Self-selection can relate to opinion, and bias does not shrink as the sample grows
Percentages from more than 10,000 people are rounded, which adds systematic error
Large samples always have larger standard errors, so the poll is less precise
The random sample has the smaller variance, so its estimate must be unbiased

rubric: Selection bias is systematic and not reduced by increasing n, while random sampling avoids it.
Distractors misstate how sample size affects error or equate small variance with unbiasedness.

items.prompt: A residual-versus-fitted plot for a linear regression shows a funnel shape: residuals spread out more as fitted values increase. Which conclusions follow? Select all that apply.

options.label: The predictor variables must be non-normal
The usual standard errors and confidence intervals may be unreliable
The error variance is not constant across fitted values
The true relationship must be nonlinear
The slope estimates are necessarily biased

rubric: A funnel indicates heteroscedasticity, which undermines standard errors that assume constant variance.
Heteroscedasticity alone does not bias OLS slopes, imply nonlinearity or concern predictor normality.

items.prompt: A product team runs an A/B test planned for 14 days. They check the p-value every morning and stop on day 5 when p = 0.03, declaring the new design a winner. A later full-length replication shows no difference. What best diagnoses the problem in the first test?

options.label: Day 5 data are unrepresentative because weekday effects usually only show up after a full week of traffic has accumulated
A p-value of 0.03 is too weak for online experiments, which usually need a threshold of 0.001 before a result is trusted
Repeated looks with a stop-on-significance rule give many chances to cross 0.05, inflating the false positive rate
The test was underpowered at the start, so a significant result at that sample size is more likely to be a false positive

rubric: Optional stopping or peeking gives many chances to cross the threshold, so the true Type I error exceeds the nominal 5%.
Distractors invoke fixed rules about days, thresholds or power rather than the stopping rule.

items.prompt: A report must describe typical household income for a region where a few households earn extremely high incomes. The criteria: the figure should reflect what a typical household earns and should not move much if one billionaire moves in. Which summary best meets them?

options.label: The mean, because it uses every observation and so is the most informative
The median, because it is resistant to a few extreme values
The mean after a log transformation, because it uses every observation and is less affected by extremes
The mode, because it is the most frequent income and ignores extreme values

rubric: The median is robust to extreme values, matching both stated criteria.
Distractors favour using all the data (mean) or confuse spread or the mode with typical value.

items.prompt: A trial measures blood pressure in the same 30 patients before and after a treatment. Patients differ greatly in baseline pressure. The goal is the most precise estimate of the treatment effect. Which analysis is best?

options.label: A paired analysis of within-patient differences, removing baseline variability
A two-sample test of before versus after groups, since randomisation to time points makes the groups comparable
A two-sample comparison of before and after groups, since it uses all 60 values and so has more power
Comparing only the group means, since individual differences average out anyway across patients

rubric: Pairing removes large baseline differences between patients, reducing variance of the estimate.
Treating the measurements as independent ignores the pairing and wastes precision.

items.prompt: An analyst reports a 95% CI for mean delivery time of (4.1, 5.9) days and writes: 'There is a 95% probability the true mean lies in this interval.' Which critique is most accurate?

options.label: It is wrong because a probability statement can only come from a p-value, never from an interval estimate
It is correct, because the interval was computed from the sample data using the 95% confidence level
It is imprecise: 95% is the long-run capture rate of the method, not a probability for this interval
It is wrong because the interval is the range that contains about 95% of individual delivery times

rubric: In the frequentist framing the parameter is fixed; 95% refers to the procedure's long-run coverage.
A distractor confuses a CI for the mean with a range covering individual observations.

items.prompt: You must compare mean task times of two groups with n = 12 each. Both samples are strongly right-skewed with two extreme outliers. The criterion: a valid inference without relying on normality. Which approach is best?

options.label: Dropping the outliers and then applying the t-test, since extreme values never carry information
A t-test with a lower alpha, because that compensates for skew in small samples
A two-sample t-test, because the central limit theorem applies whenever n is at least 10
A permutation or rank-based test, because it does not rely on a normal sampling distribution

rubric: With small skewed samples, a permutation or rank test avoids the normality assumption.
Distractors misapply the CLT, delete data arbitrarily, or think alpha fixes distributional problems.

items.prompt: You must compare response-time distributions across 5 servers. Each has a long right tail of slow requests spanning several orders of magnitude, and the audience needs to see median, spread and tail behaviour. Which display is best?

options.label: A bar chart of mean response time per server with error bars, giving one comparable number each
A pie chart of each server's share of total requests, which is easy to read
A single pooled histogram on a linear scale, which shows all the requests at once
Side-by-side box plots on a log scale, showing medians, quartiles and tails per server

rubric: Box plots on a log scale compare location, spread and tails for several skewed groups.
Mean bars hide tails, pies show shares not distributions, and a pooled linear histogram hides group differences.

items.prompt: A study with 50,000 participants reports 'p = 0.003, so the effect on test scores is important.' Which are valid criticisms of this conclusion? Select all that apply.

options.label: With a very large n, even a trivially small effect can give a small p-value
A p-value does not measure the size or practical importance of an effect
A p of 0.003 means there is a 99.7% chance the effect is real, so the study should have reported a stricter threshold
A p-value below 0.05 guarantees the result will replicate, so the single study is enough to call it important
A small p-value proves the study had no confounding, so the effect must be causal and therefore important

rubric: Significance and importance differ; a large n makes tiny effects significant, so effect size and CI are needed.
Other options misinterpret p as the probability the effect is real, or as proof of no bias or replication.

items.prompt: A city has three districts: A (60% of residents, fairly uniform incomes), B (30%, moderately varied) and C (10%, extremely varied). With a budget for 600 interviews, officials want a precise city-wide income estimate and usable estimates for each district. Which design best meets both criteria?

options.label: Simple random sampling of 600 residents citywide, since it gives every resident an equal chance and needs no weighting
Interviewing the 600 most accessible residents, since cooperative respondents give cleaner and more complete data
Stratified random sampling by district with enough interviews in each, then weighted to the city total
Cluster sampling of one whole district, since that minimises travel cost and gives a deep picture of local incomes

rubric: Stratifying guarantees district-level samples (including small, variable C) and weighting gives valid city-wide estimates.
Simple random sampling may leave district C with too few cases; convenience and one-district cluster samples are biased.

items.prompt: A report states: "There is a 95% probability that the true mean lies in our computed interval (2.1, 4.9)." Which evaluation is best under standard frequentist inference?

options.label: The wording is flawed, because the 95% refers to the long-run capture rate of the method, while the fixed true mean is either in this interval or not
The wording is fine, because the sample mean sits at the centre of the interval and so the true mean is 95% likely to be near it
The wording is fine, because a 95% interval always equals a Bayesian posterior interval, so the probability applies to this interval directly
The wording is flawed, because the 95% only tells us the share of individual observations falling inside the interval, not where the mean is

rubric: The confidence level describes the procedure's long-run coverage; the parameter is fixed, so no probability attaches to one computed interval.
Distractors confuse confidence intervals with posterior intervals or with the spread of individual observations.

items.prompt: A study tests 20 subgroups for a treatment effect at alpha = 0.05. One subgroup shows p = 0.03, the rest are non-significant. Which judgement is best?

options.label: Report it as a confirmed effect, because p = 0.03 is below 0.05 and the subgroup was a natural category already present in the data
Treat it as exploratory: with 20 tests about one false positive is expected, so confirm it in new data or adjust for multiplicity
Loosen the subgroup threshold to 0.10, because smaller subgroups have less power and therefore deserve a more lenient cut-off for claims
Discard every result from the study, because running more than one test on the same dataset invalidates all of the p-values it yields

rubric: With 20 tests at 5%, one nominally significant result is expected by chance, so it needs replication or multiplicity adjustment.
Distractors either ignore multiplicity or overcorrect by discarding everything.

items.prompt: You have 40 household incomes, strongly right-skewed with three extreme values. The goal is to describe the typical household with honest uncertainty. Which approach best meets those criteria?

options.label: The median with a bootstrap percentile interval, because it targets the typical household and does not rely on normality or extremes
The mode with a normal-approximation interval, because the most frequent income best describes a typical household in skewed data sets
The mean after deleting the highest values, so the normality assumption holds and the interval becomes narrower and more precise overall
The mean with a t-interval, because the t-interval is exact at any sample size once the standard deviation has been estimated from data

rubric: The median resists outliers and a bootstrap interval avoids normality assumptions at n = 40.
Deleting values biases the estimate; the t-interval assumes near-normality, which skew and n = 40 undermine.

items.prompt: A test on 2,000,000 users finds a mean score difference of 0.02 points on a 100-point scale (SD about 15), p < 0.001. A manager wants to ship the change. Which response is best?

options.label: Conclude the effect is strong, because p < 0.001 means the difference is very large and almost certainly big in size as well as statistically real
Lower alpha to 0.0001 and retest, because a stricter significance threshold will show whether the difference is large enough to matter in practice
Reject the result outright, because any sample this large must contain hidden bias that makes every p-value meaningless regardless of the study design
Report the effect size with its confidence interval and judge whether 0.02 points matters in practice, since huge n makes tiny effects significant

rubric: Significance is not importance; with enormous n a trivial effect gives a tiny p-value, so the effect size and interval matter.
Distractors equate p with effect size or misuse alpha as a measure of importance.

items.prompt: To estimate a national proportion, option X is a voluntary web poll with 50,000 responses; option Y is a random sample of 800 with a 95% response rate. Judged on trustworthiness of the estimate, which is best?

options.label: Pool X and Y, because the combined n is largest and the random portion will correct the bias that the voluntary responses introduce
Option X, because its very large sample makes the standard error tiny enough to offset any selection effect from self-chosen respondents
Neither, because a proportion for a national population can only be estimated from a full census rather than from any sample at all
Option Y, because selection bias does not shrink as n grows while the small random sample has a known and quantifiable sampling error

rubric: Bias from self-selection persists at any n; a random sample with high response gives an unbiased estimate with known error.
Distractors trust sheer size or assume pooling averages away bias.

items.prompt: A team checks an A/B test daily and stops the first day p < 0.05 under a fixed-sample t-test. Which criticisms are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: Effects estimated at an early stop tend to be overstated, since stopping favours lucky random swings
Stopping early only costs power and never affects the false-positive rate, so the main risk is missing real effects
Peeking is harmless provided the final sample is large, because the law of large numbers restores the error rate
The p-value at the stopping time no longer carries its nominal meaning under a fixed-sample design
Repeated looks at accumulating data push the overall false-positive rate well above 5%

rubric: Optional stopping inflates type I error, invalidates nominal p-values and biases the stopped estimate upward.
Distractors claim large n or power considerations remove the problem, which they do not.

items.prompt: Hospital A has a 90% overall survival rate and Hospital B 85%. Within mild cases and within severe cases separately, B has the higher survival rate, but B treats far more severe cases. A regulator must advise a patient of known severity on which hospital shows better quality. Which judgement is best?

options.label: Rank them equal, because the overall and subgroup differences cancel out once averaged across hospitals and severity levels together
Rank A higher, because the overall rate uses every patient and is therefore the most complete and least biased measure of quality
Call the data contradictory, because an overall result and its subgroup results cannot disagree unless a calculation error exists somewhere
Rank B higher for like-for-like patients, because severity confounds the overall rates and the stratified comparison shows B doing better

rubric: This is Simpson's paradox: case mix confounds the pooled rates, so the severity-stratified comparison is the relevant one.
Distractors treat pooled data as automatically correct or claim the reversal is impossible.

items.prompt: You will sample 200 units in total to estimate an overall mean, at equal cost per unit. Strata: A (N = 5000, SD 2), B (N = 3000, SD 10), C (N = 2000, SD 5). Which allocation to A, B, C minimises the variance of the estimate?
rubric: Neyman allocation is proportional to N times SD: 10000, 30000, 10000, giving 40, 120, 40.
Proportional allocation (100, 60, 40) ignores variability; equal allocation ignores size and variability.

items.prompt: A cluster-sampled poll must give a 95% margin of error of at most 3 percentage points for a proportion, using worst-case p = 0.5 and z = 1.96. Clustering gives a design effect of 1.5. What is the smallest sample size, to the nearest hundred, that meets the constraint?
rubric: Simple random sampling needs 1.96^2 * 0.25 / 0.03^2, about 1,068; multiplying by 1.5 gives about 1,601.
1,068 ignores the design effect; 712 divides by it; 2,401 corresponds to a 2-point margin.

items.prompt: A trial randomises 12 classrooms (6 per arm) to a teaching method, with 25 students tested in each. Which analysis plan best respects the design and the independence constraint?

options.label: Compare classroom means, or fit a mixed model with a classroom random effect, so the analysis unit matches the randomised unit
Run a t-test on all 300 students as independent observations, since a larger number of observations raises power for the same true effect
Run 12 separate tests, one per classroom, and count how many are significant to decide whether the method worked overall
Drop any classroom whose mean differs sharply from its arm's average, so that between-classroom noise is reduced before the t-test

rubric: Students within a classroom are correlated and randomisation was at classroom level, so analysis must be at that level or model the clustering.
Treating students as independent inflates the false-positive rate; trimming classrooms is arbitrary.

items.prompt: A product team wants to look at an experiment weekly for up to four weeks and stop early for a clear win, while keeping the overall false-positive rate at 5%. Which plan meets both constraints?

options.label: Test at 0.05 each week and stop at the first significant result, since every individual test is valid at the 5% level
Test at 0.05 each week but stop only if the effect also exceeds a size chosen after seeing the first week's data
Pre-specify four looks with an alpha-spending boundary such as O'Brien-Fleming so the total type I error stays at 5%
Look weekly but average the four p-values and compare the mean with 0.05, since averaging removes the multiplicity problem

rubric: Group sequential designs spend the 5% alpha across planned looks, allowing early stopping with controlled error.
Distractors keep nominal 0.05 per look, choose thresholds post hoc, or average p-values, which is not valid.

items.prompt: A proposal estimates the prevalence of a condition expected near 1% from a simple random sample of 200 people, and promises a 95% interval of about plus or minus 0.3 percentage points. What is the design missing?

options.label: A continuity correction, because proportions near 1% are discrete and always need that adjustment to reach the stated precision
A sample size sized to the precision goal: about 4,200 are needed, whereas 200 yields only about two expected cases
A stratification by age band, since a simple random sample cannot estimate any proportion without separate strata for every age group
A one-sided interval, because prevalence cannot be negative and so a two-sided interval wastes half of the available sample size

rubric: n = 1.96^2 * 0.01 * 0.99 / 0.003^2 is about 4,200, so 200 people cannot deliver the promised precision.
Other options propose adjustments that do not address the core precision shortfall.

items.prompt: Patients are nested in 15 clinics, and you must build a 95% bootstrap interval for the overall median outcome that respects the clustering. Which design elements are needed? Select all that apply.

options.label: Recompute the median on every resample and take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of those medians
Divide the bootstrap standard error by the square root of the patient count to account for clustering
Resample clinics with replacement, keeping each sampled clinic's patients together as a unit
Replace the median with the mean so a normal-theory standard error can be used on each resample
Resample all patients pooled and independent of clinic, to maximise the effective sample size

rubric: A cluster bootstrap resamples clinics and takes percentiles of the recomputed statistic across resamples.
Pooling patients ignores within-clinic correlation and gives intervals that are too narrow.

items.prompt: A satisfaction survey has 30% non-response, and there is reason to think unhappy customers respond less often. You must report an overall satisfaction estimate that is defensible. Which plan best meets that constraint?

options.label: Report the mean of respondents only, since the large number of responses received keeps the estimate close to the population value
Fill in each missing score with the respondent mean, since that keeps the average unchanged and makes the sample appear complete, so no further adjustment is needed
Follow up a random subsample of non-respondents intensively and weight them up, then run sensitivity analyses on plausible missing-data biases
Delete the 30% of the lowest-scoring respondents to match, since that balances the missing unhappy customers with the removed ones

rubric: When missingness depends on the outcome, follow-up of a random non-respondent subsample plus sensitivity analysis addresses the bias directly.
Respondent-only means and mean imputation keep the bias; deleting respondents adds a new one.
